newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks heart surgery to let him work harder.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks heart surgery to let him work harder.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said in an interview published on Monday that he had opted to have heart surgery because the Russian people expected him to be able to work without sparing himself.

In an interview with the weekly Itogi current affairs magazine, Yeltsin said he disliked discussing his health but that the support of his fellow-countrymen, who returned him to power on July 3, gave them the right to know about it.
"No normal person likes public discussions of his own illnesses," Yeltsin, 65, said in written answers which editor Sergei Parkhomenko said were received last Wednesday.
"But citizens of the Russian Federation have entrusted me with the post of the president...It is an enormous honour...but a heavy burden as well."
"Part of it is the realisation that from the moment of taking the oath...you do not belong to yourself or your family any more. There are no more personal problems, all of them become political."
Last Thursday, Yeltsin broke more than two months of silence by announcing in a television interview that he had decided to have heart surgery to be able to return to "active" life.

Top cardiologist Yevgeny Chazov said on Monday a council of doctors would meet at the end of September to decide who would carry out the operation, expected to be a heart bypass, Interfax news agency said.

Such councils are traditionally called before any top official undergoes surgery. But the timing of the session raised the possibility that the surgery itself might take place later than at the end of the month as Yeltsin had said.
His absence from public life had triggered speculation, in the media and in the markets, about his state of health and ability to control the country of 150 million people.

During last week's television appearance, he spoke slowly but with glimmers of his old sparkle. He is known to be at his best in a crisis and he appeared somewhat relieved after taking the decision to go under the knife.
In the Itogi magazine, Yeltsin appeared to be even more emphatic than during his television performance.
"I am sure that one month ago the Russian people...voted for a president who...will serve the Motherland without sparing himself."
"I am being told -- take care of yourself, go easy. I cannot go easy on myself...I was elected not to go easy on myself, I have been elected to work. That is why I think I need the operation."
Yeltsin's personal friend, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said after visiting the Kremlin leader at a hunting lodge outside Moscow on Saturday that Yeltsin was "very optimistic" about the operation.
Itogi's Parkhomenko told Reuters on Friday that he thought Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was the man who changed the president's mind when he visited him last Monday.
"He must have told Yeltsin: 'Look, the same surgeon did the same operation on me in 1992 and here I am, alive and fit'," Parkhomenko said.
Moscow's Cardiological Centre, headed by Chazov, conducted "coronorography" tests on the president in mid-August which showed the need for an operation on the blood vessels supplying his heart.

But Yeltsin initially refused to have surgery, Parkhomenko said. He quoted several doctors who said such behaviour was typical for many patients, especially those in responsible posts with a strong will and a desire to lead.
Moreover, most of the best Russian heart surgeons refused to operate on Yeltsin, for fear of failure, Parkhomenko said.
But one, Professor Rinat Akchurin, the chief surgeon at Chazov's centre, said: "I will do it, I did the same for Chernomyrdin in 1992".
